Catalog Kids Methodology

Methodology

What the number means.

Acuity asks one question of every title: how much does watching this enrich the mind behind your eyes? Not how popular it is, not how long it keeps you on the couch — how much it gives back. Here is exactly how we turn that question into a score.

One scale, three dimensions

Every film and series is graded on three independent dimensions, each from 0 to 100:

Depth

How much the title asks of you — structural complexity, ambiguity, layered plotting, and ideas that reward a second pass. High scores demand attention.

Insight

What you carry out of it — history, science, character of a real place or person, a discipline made legible. How much you simply know that you didn't before.

Craft

Whether the thing is actually made well — writing, performance, direction, and the cohesion that separates a considered work from a competent one.

The three dimensions are blended into a single composite, then placed on a wide, IQ-style scale we call the Acuity Quotient — a deliberate nod to a familiar standardized measure. The median title sits at 100 and the scale runs up to roughly 200. The number is a measure of a title's cognitive value, not a ranking position — and because the scale is anchored to the whole catalog, it recalibrates as the catalog grows: add thousands more titles and every score is re-derived from the same method, so a 130 means the same thing tomorrow as it does today.

A deliberately flattened curve

Most rating sites drift upward until almost everything is "great" and the scale stops meaning anything. We do the opposite — but we also refuse the other trap, the tall central spike that buries every title in the middle. The Acuity Quotient is calibrated into a single, bell-shaped hump centered on a median of 100, with a standard deviation of about 37. It is intentionally flatter than a normal distribution: we push real weight outward toward the ends, so the top and bottom of the scale are populated rather than empty. Most titles still cluster near the middle, but genuine brilliance and genuine noise both have room to live in tails that actually carry titles.

This is the credibility test for the whole project, so we show our work. Here is the distribution of every Acuity Quotient in the catalog:

Each bar is the number of titles at a given Acuity Quotient, colored by the tier that score falls into. A near-zero skew keeps the hump symmetric, while the flattened shape and weighted tails keep the ends of the scale from emptying out. Click a tier in the key to isolate its band.

The five tiers

Numbers are precise but cold, so each title also falls into one of five named bands, drawn by fixed cut-points on the scale and color-coded consistently everywhere on the site. The names describe how much a title asks of you — from Idle background to something genuinely Profound.

Where the facts come from

The factual scaffolding — titles, years, genres, audience ratings, and vote counts — is drawn from public IMDb datasets. Streaming availability reflects US services and is illustrative; when a title has no availability on record, we say so rather than guess. The scores themselves are ours: computed by a single, repeatable method from those public signals, never hand-tuned title by title.

Because one canonical dataset drives every page, a title's number is identical wherever you meet it — the catalog, its detail page, a head-to-head comparison. Update the data, and the whole site updates with it. There is no second, editorial set of numbers hiding behind the first.

What it is not

A high Acuity Quotient is not a command and a low one is not an insult. Comfort viewing earns a low cognitive load by design, and that is a perfectly good reason to watch something. Acuity is a measuring instrument, not a verdict on your taste — its only job is to tell you, plainly, what a given hour is likely to give back.

Sources & credits

The factual layer beneath every score comes from public datasets, and we credit it plainly. Title metadata — names, release years, genres, audience ratings, and vote counts — is drawn from IMDb's public datasets and is used here for non-commercial purposes only. Poster artwork is served directly from TMDB's image servers and is never downloaded or rehosted: we simply hotlink each image so the credit and the bytes both stay with their source.

This product uses the TMDB API but is not endorsed or certified by TMDB. The Acuity Quotient, its three dimensions, and the tiers are our own computed work, layered on top of these public facts — the numbers are ours, the underlying data is theirs.
